questions.question: What is the typical percentage of memory references that are writes in general workloads?
questions.explanation:
Experience shows that about 15% of memory references are writes in typical applications. (Source Page: [24])  

---

questions.question: For high‑performance computing applications such as vector‑vector multiplication, the write percentage can approach which value?
questions.explanation:
HPC workloads like vector‑vector multiplication may have write references around 33%. (Source Page: [24])  

---

questions.question: In the cache associativity diagram, which term describes a cache with four possible locations for a block within a set?
questions.explanation:
The diagram lists “Four-way” as one of the associativity options. (Source Page: [23])  

---

questions.question: In a write‑back cache, when is a replaced block written back to main memory?

options.A: Every time a block is replaced
options.B: Only if the block is clean
options.C: Only if the dirty bit is set
options.D: Never; write‑back never writes to memory on replacement

questions.explanation:
A block is written back only when its dirty bit indicates it has been modified. (Source Page: [24])  

---

questions.question: What is a major drawback of write‑back caches concerning I/O module accesses?

options.A: They increase cache hit rate for I/O accesses.
options.B: Portions of main memory become invalid, forcing I/O to go through the cache and creating potential bottlenecks.
options.C: They eliminate the need for a dirty bit.
options.D: They automatically synchronize with I/O devices.

questions.explanation:
Because written‑back data may not be in main memory, I/O modules must access memory via the cache, adding complexity and possible bottlenecks. (Source Page: [24])  

---

questions.question: Which write policy is most commonly used together with write‑back caching?
questions.explanation:
Write back is typically paired with write allocate to keep subsequent writes hitting the cache. (Source Page: [25])  

---

questions.question: Which processor family is cited as supporting “no write allocate” as an option?
questions.explanation:
The ARM Cortex architecture allows a no‑write‑allocate policy. (Source Page: [25])  

---

questions.question: According to the simplified Pentium 4 diagram, how many major components make up the processor core?
questions.explanation:
The text states the core consists of four major components. (Source Page: [31])

questions.question: The Pentium 4 cache architecture discussed is similar to that of modern x86 systems. How many distinct cache levels are highlighted in the diagram?
questions.explanation:
The figure emphasizes the placement of three caches (L1, L2, L3). (Source Page: [31])

questions.question: What advantage does write allocate provide after a cache miss on a write?

options.A: It forces the write to bypass the cache, reducing traffic.
options.B: It stores the written data only in main memory.
options.C: Subsequent writes to the same block will hit in the cache and set the dirty bit.
options.D: It converts the cache to a write‑through policy automatically.

questions.explanation: Write allocate brings the block into the cache, so later writes hit and the block becomes dirty. (Source Page: [25])
